title: LCA of Integrated Multi-Trophic Aquaculture (IMTA): Fish, Oysters and Macroalgae in Earthen Ponds
sub: A comparison of two pond IMTA systems with a conventional fish-only pond, based on published farm data from the INTEGRATE project, with a 13-KPI decision framework for environment and circularity.
pdf: Case 11 — LCA of Integrated Multi-Trophic Aquaculture (IMTA): Executive Summary
disc: Published project data. Inventory, nutrient balance and impact results are from INTEGRATE deliverable PI05#3 (IPMA & CTAQUA, 2020), based on records from experimental farm ponds and calculated with Piscentool. The scaling, data checks and KPI framework come from the author's open repository. This is not a certified LCA or a CSRD disclosure.

boundary: Cradle-to-farm-gate: fry and spat, feed ingredients and processing, farm energy, water use, equipment, buildings, vehicles, chemicals, transport to the farm, direct land and water occupation, and N and P emissions to water. Packaging, transport to retail, consumption and end-of-life excluded
geo: Olhão, Ria Formosa, Portugal (SI-POLY, SI-IMTA) and Cádiz, Spain (SE-IMTA)
time: SI-IMTA May–Oct 2017 (5.3 months); SE-IMTA Jan–Nov 2019 (8.5 months); SI-POLY May 2017–Jul 2019 (26 months). Report 2020; KPI layer 2026
method: Piscentool (Wilfart et al., 2012) with SimaPro background data: GWP100, total cumulative energy demand, net primary production use, acidification (kg SO₂ eq), eutrophication (kg PO₄ eq), land competition and water dependence. Categories differ from the EF 3.1 set used in cases 1–10
alloc: No allocation between fish and oysters (summed by mass in the functional unit). Macroalgae are an associated downstream product outside the functional unit, with no allocation and no credit. Shared infrastructure, vehicles and electricity allocated by production-pond area / total farm pond area
cutoff: As in the report: packaging and post-farm stages excluded; all farm inputs included
dq: Primary data from daily farm records (water flow, aeration, feed, mortality, treatments) and feed-manufacturer data, as published. 37 of 39 cross-checks between report tables pass; two open issues are documented in the repository
srcShort: INTEGRATE deliverable PI05#3 (IPMA & CTAQUA, 2020), Tables 4–5 and Annex 1; scaling and KPIs from the author's IMTA repository.
loop: Nutrient loop: oysters filter particles and macroalgae take up dissolved N and P released by the fed fish
lciNote: Inventory per tonne of product for the three systems (SI-POLY / SI-IMTA / SE-IMTA). Data type P = primary farm data as published in the report · D = derived (recalculated in the repository). Background datasets (Piscentool/SimaPro) are not redistributed.
exec:
This case study compares two integrated multi-trophic aquaculture (IMTA) systems with a conventional fish-only pond, using published farm data from the INTEGRATE project (Interreg Atlantic Area). In IMTA, fed fish are combined with oysters, which filter particles, and macroalgae, which take up dissolved nutrients. The question is whether this circular design also lowers life-cycle impacts.
Per tonne of fish and oyster flesh, the fish-only pond emits 2,836 kg CO2e and releases 96 kg of nitrogen to water. Feed is the hotspot in every system: it causes 55–66% of global warming and almost all primary production use. In the semi-intensive ponds, uneaten feed and excretion drive 60–84% of acidification and eutrophication, and pumping drives most energy use.
The semi-intensive IMTA keeps global warming almost unchanged (−1%), but cuts eutrophication by 57% and water dependence by 58%. Nearly half of the feed nitrogen ends up in fish, oysters and macroalgae, compared with 20% in the fish-only pond. The semi-extensive, tidal IMTA cuts global warming by 56%, energy by 81% and eutrophication by 97%. The trade-off is land: both IMTA systems need more area per tonne.
Recommendations focus on feed efficiency, tidal or low-energy water exchange and valorising macroalgae. For reporting, the results map to ESRS E1, E2, E3 (marine resources), E4 and E5.
overview:
The three systems are earthen ponds in southern Portugal and Spain. SI-POLY is a semi-intensive polyculture of meagre and gilthead seabream with pumped seawater (the conventional baseline). SI-IMTA adds Pacific oysters and Ulva macroalgae to a similar semi-intensive pond. SE-IMTA is a semi-extensive system with gilthead seabream and oysters, a second pond with macroalgae fed by the fishpond outflow, and tidal water exchange.
The repository re-uses the INTEGRATE inventory and per-process impact results, recalculates the nitrogen and phosphorus balance, checks the report tables against each other and turns the results into 13 KPIs with targets.
goal: The goal is to compare the potential environmental impacts of two pond IMTA designs with a fish-only pond, identify hotspots and translate the results into KPIs that support a farm-design decision. The intended audience is project partners, researchers, farm operators and policymakers working on sustainable aquaculture. The systems differ in site, species and cycle length, so results compare real systems rather than single design variables.

hot.why: Feed causes 55–66% of global warming and over 99% of net primary production use in every system, and most land competition in the semi-intensive ponds (66–80%). Feed efficiency is the main lever.
Nitrogen and phosphorus released from the semi-intensive ponds cause 60–84% of acidification and eutrophication. Extractive species reduce this directly.
Pumping and aeration cause 66% of energy demand in the fish-only pond and 51% in the semi-intensive IMTA, but almost nothing with tidal exchange.
IMTA needs more pond area per tonne: direct land occupation is 32% of land competition in SI-IMTA and 86% in SE-IMTA.

hot.t: Equipment and buildings in short cycles
hot.why: Short experimental cycles (5.3 and 8.5 months) spread infrastructure over little output, giving about 19% of global warming in both IMTA systems.

desc: Meagre + gilthead seabream, pumped seawater, Olhão, 26-month cycle
Meagre, white seabream, mullet + oysters + Ulva, pumped seawater, Olhão, 5.3-month cycle
Gilthead seabream + oysters, macroalgae pond, tidal exchange, Cádiz, 8.5-month cycle

sens.xl: Fish feed conversion ratio (kg feed per kg fish gain)
sens.yl: kg CO₂e per tonne of product
sens.note: Not in the report: the Feeds process is scaled linearly with feed amount using the report's implied factor (about 1.05 kg CO2e per kg feed for SI-POLY and 1.01 for SI-IMTA). All other processes held at reported values. Reported FCRs are 1.79 and 1.72.
sens.interp: Each 0.1 improvement in feed conversion saves about 90–105 kg CO2e per tonne. Feed efficiency matters more for global warming than adding extractive species to a semi-intensive pond.

ci.stage: Feed dominates global warming in the fish-only pond; farm energy and transports follow. Process values are rounded in the report, so the sum (2,835) differs by 1 from the reported total (2,836).
ci.stage_e: Pumping and aeration energy causes two thirds of energy demand in the fish-only pond.
ci.stage_w: Water dependence is almost entirely the seawater passing through the ponds and direct pond occupation.
ci.donut: Feed alone accounts for about two thirds of the climate result, so feed formulation and feed efficiency are the first levers.
ci.sankey: In the semi-intensive IMTA, 47% of feed nitrogen is retained in fish, oysters and macroalgae; 53% is released to water. In the fish-only pond, 80% is released.
ci.heat: Feed is a hotspot across climate, land and primary production use; rejects for eutrophication and acidification; pumping for energy; direct activity for water and land.
ci.scen: Global warming falls mainly where less feed and no pumping are needed (semi-extensive IMTA). Adding oysters and macroalgae to a semi-intensive pond barely changes global warming.
ci.scenNote: The three systems differ in site, species and cycle length; they are real systems, not single-variable scenarios.
ci.radar: Both IMTA systems shrink on six of seven axes; land competition is the one category where the fish-only pond is better.
ci.wf: Lower feed per tonne and tidal water exchange explain most of the difference between the fish-only pond and the semi-extensive IMTA; infrastructure in the short cycle adds some impact back.

interp.m: IMTA keeps nutrients in the system: oysters and macroalgae turn released nitrogen and phosphorus into products, which sharply reduces eutrophication. Large climate and energy savings come from lower-input, tidal designs rather than from extractive species alone.
interp.a: Feed amount and composition; water-exchange method; cycle length and stocking density; allocation of shared infrastructure by pond area; macroalgae outside the functional unit.
interp.u: Experimental ponds with short and different cycle lengths; rounded Annex 1 values; land competition of SI-POLY does not follow the report's rule; basis of macroalgae weights unclear; fry modelled with a carp-fry proxy.
interp.can: Feed and nutrient release are the main hotspots; IMTA lowers eutrophication and water dependence; tidal semi-extensive systems have much lower climate and energy impacts per tonne, with more land use.
interp.cannot: Results cannot be generalised to commercial-scale farms without longer cycles and more data, and they do not value the macroalgae co-product or biodiversity effects on the coastal ecosystem.
interp.d: Farm design (species mix, water exchange), feed procurement and formulation, nutrient-management targets, site planning that weighs land use against nutrient benefits.

recs: For farm designers: combine fed species with extractive species sized to the nutrient load, and prefer gravity or tidal water exchange where the site allows.
Buy feed with lower fishmeal and fish-oil inclusion and verified responsible sourcing; track feed conversion per batch.
For feed producers: publish product carbon footprints and improve digestibility to reduce nitrogen excretion.
Develop markets for oysters and macroalgae so that extractive co-products earn revenue.
Not directly relevant; for sediment and sludge, explore nutrient recovery.
Track nitrogen and phosphorus use efficiency, net nutrient release and feed share of emissions as KPIs alongside GHG per tonne.
Recognise nutrient extraction by IMTA in water-quality and licensing frameworks; support marketing standards for macroalgae.

take: IMTA keeps nutrients in the system rather than in coastal water: adding oysters and macroalgae cuts eutrophication by more than half, while the large climate savings come from low-input, tidal designs and better feed efficiency.
biz: Design ponds around feed efficiency and low-energy water exchange, size extractive species to the nutrient load, build markets for oysters and macroalgae, and track nutrient-use efficiency alongside GHG per tonne.
assume: Real farm data from experimental ponds as reported in INTEGRATE PI05#3; functional unit 1 t fish + oyster flesh; macroalgae outside the functional unit; infrastructure allocated by pond area; impact categories from Piscentool (not EF 3.1), so results are not directly comparable with cases 1–10.
